newsitem.title: GERMANY: Germany risks importing inflation with weak mark.
newsitem.headline: Germany risks importing inflation with weak mark.

text.p: The battered deutschemark is fanning worries that price pressures will rise in Germany as foreign goods and materials become more expensive for German firms.
Data on Friday showed that while import prices fell 0.2 percent on a month-on-month basis in June, the yearly rate rose to 3.3 percent from 2.8 percent in May -- the highest annual rise in six years.
Economists say this is a sign of things to come.

"We have had quite a significant further decline in the deutschemark since June and people will be looking to see how that effects import price data going forward," said Ros Lifton, senior international economist at HSBC Markets in London.

Lifton said that she estimated the average dollar/mark exchange had been around 1.73 marks in June. Since then, the mark has lost another 10 pfennigs in value -- trading at six-year lows at around 1.84 to the dollar in recent sessions.
"Clearly we are going to see further rises in import prices," said Lifton.

For the Bundesbank, the question is whether pipeline price pressure will spell real danger for headline inflation. Its key interest rates have remained historically low for 15 months -- the longest period since the mid- to late-1970s.

"The Bundesbank is in a very difficult situation," said Armin Kayser, economist at SBC Warburg in Frankfurt. "If they look at the precepitous decline of the mark and rising import prices, a pre-emptive move on rates would be justified."
"But at the same time, the domestic economy looks pretty fragile and it is hard to see them punishing the adjustment process which is underway in Germany."

Dresdner Kleinwort Bension economist Stefan Bergheim said Germany had entered a period of two-tier inflation, with all price indicators which depend heavily of the mark's value showing consistent upward pressure, while high street prices remained subdued.

Pointing to the mark's continuous depreciation over the past few years and the relatively muted effect on headline inflation, Bergheim said he expected this two-tier pattern to continue, presenting no immediate threat of a rise in interest rates.
But Kayser said that with the trade-weighted value of the mark around 8.0 percent lower in July this year than in July 1996, import prices were set for a pretty hefty rise in the coming months.
"There is a significant risk that this will raise import prices by as much as five percent -- we could be heading for that kind of (year-on-year) figure by the autumn," he said.

Germany's annual inflation rate is still comfortably below 2.0 percent. Although the direct effect of the sufferings of the mark on consumer price inflation has been minimal so far, Kayser said he could not believe that such a sharp rise would not filter through to high street prices soon.
"And I guess that this would not leave the Bundesbank totally unimpressed," he said.
HSBC's Lifton, however, said much of the sting of higher import prices could well be taken out at factory gate.

She pointed first to falling commodity and oil prices in dollar and mark terms on a year-on-year basis, saying this meant the actual imported cost pressure through raw materials was not as painful as it could be.
"And unit wage costs are going to fall this year, which will allow companies plenty of scope to offset any increase in input costs via a reduction in labour costs," she said.
